CALL AND NOTICE OF SPECIAL MEETING

To the Members of the City Council of the City of Palos Verdes Estates:

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the Mayor has called a special meeting of the City Council to
take place at City Hall, 340 Palos Verdes Drive West, Palos Verdes Estates, CA at 5:45 p.m. on
Tuesday, September 26, 2017. The agenda for the special meeting with the items of business to be
transacted or discussed is set forth below.

Posted by the Office of the City Clerk on September 22, 2017, at 5:00 p.m.

Copies of the staff reports or other written documentation relating to each item of business referred to
on the agenda are on file in the office of the City Clerk and are available for public inspection. If
applicable, materials related to an item on this agenda submitted to the Council after distribution of the
agenda packet are available for public inspection in the City Clerk’s office during normal business
hours. Any person having any question concerning any agenda item may call the City Clerk to make
inquiry concerning the item. Upon request, the agenda and documents in the agenda packet can be
made available in appropriate alternative formats to persons with a disability in compliance with the
Americans with Disabilities Act. Please contact the City Clerk at 310-378-0383, at least 48 hours
prior to the meeting to request a disability-related modification or accommodation.

The City Council welcomes and encourages public participation at the Council meetings; however,
to allow for the orderly progression of business, each person wishing to comment or make a
presentation shall be limited to three (3) minutes. Anyone wishing to address the City Council is
requested to fill out a green speaker’s card available at the end of each row in the Chambers. The
card permits the City to identify persons for purposes of City Council minute preparation. The City

TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL

THRU:  ANTON DAHLERBRUCH, CITY MANAGER /s/

FROM:  KARINA BAÑALES, ADMINISTRATIVE ANALYST – HR /s/

SUBJECT: WORKSHOP DISCUSSION ON THE CITYS WORKERS’
  COMPENSATION PROGRAM

DATE:  SEPTEMBER 26, 2017

BACKGROUND

The City of Palos Verdes Estates is insured through a joint powers municipal self-insurance
pool. The pool is comprised of member cities of the California Joint Powers Insurance
Authority (CJPIA) from throughout the state. The City's membership with the CJPIA provides
liability insurance as well as valuable training programs to help identify exposures and to
prevent losses. Among them, includes administration of the City's safety and Workers'
Compensation program.

This workshop will provide an overview of workers' compensation laws (WC), benefits and
tools that are used to effectively manage claims. In addition, the workshop will include an
explanation of the types of claims allowed under WC laws, the importance of transitional
return-to-work programs, reporting "red flags" to reduce malingering and fraud, and what
happens after a claim is filed.

Other topics to be addressed in the workshop will include the benefits available to injured
employees, claims investigations, overview of the medical and legal processes and where the
City of Palos Verdes Estates is within the pool.

  Agenda Item #: 2
  Meeting Date: September 26, 2017

TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL

FROM:  ANTON DAHLERBRUCH, CITY MANAGER /s/

SUBJECT: WORKSHOP DISCUSSION ABOUT USE OF, AND IMPROVEMENTS
  TO, PV STABLE PROPERTY AND THE EXTENSION OF
  CONCESSION AGREEMENT

DATE:  SEPTEMBER 26, 2017

ISSUE

How shall the City address the use of PV Stables property, and the extension of the
concessionaire operations and management of the PV Stables, as of February 28, 2019 when
the existing agreement concludes?

BACKGROUND

The Palos Verdes Stables (Stables) was originally established in 1926, approximately 13-years
before the City’s incorporation. The Stables are located at 4057 Via Opata on 3 and 1/2 acres
of City-owned parkland. According to the Palos Verdes Homes Association’s deed
restrictions, the Stables property (designated as area F) is established for public use and
business use, and a riding academy is authorized on the property.

There are a variety of public and private stables throughout the Palos Verdes Peninsula. Palos
Verdes Stables (Stables) is the only stable facility in Palos Verdes Estates. Adjacent to Rolling
Hills Estates, the Stables is connected by a vast network of equestrian trails in the neighboring
City(ies) for trail riding.

The City has a history of operating the Palos Verdes Stables as a City department and under a
license/concession agreement with private parties. A review of City reports indicates license
agreements existed from at least 1958 through 1982 (24 years). Between 1983 and 2000 (17
years), the Stables was operated as a City department and staffed by City employees. Since

  Page 1 of 6

  001
 2000, the facility has been operated and managed by a concessionaire. A report indicates that
a reason for the City’s direct operation of the facility in 1983 was to perform capital
improvements that were not a priority, although they were the responsibility, of the prior
concessionaires.

The City improved the property between 1983 and 2000 with the construction of several new
barns. However, the cost of operating and maintaining the facility (including depreciation on
capital assets) resulted in continuing financial losses to the City. The City had accrued deficits
both in terms of (1) annual operations (cumulative, multi-year deficit of $74,601) and (2)
capital asset depreciation (cumulative, multi-year deficit of $169,191). Accordingly, these
deficits were reflected in audited financial statements.

Contract with RCG Management

After an extensive process in September 2000 (Attachment A to this report provides a Los
Angeles Times report on this matter), the City Council approved a concession agreement with
RCG Management, Inc. for stable operation services. The concession agreement required the
concessionaire to maintain the property and operate/manage the stable facilities for the
recreational use and benefit of the residents of Palos Verdes Estates, those persons who board
horses at the property, and any other users of the stable. Over the subsequent eight years, RCG
made concession payments to the City that eliminated the previously accrued $74,601
operating deficit. Additionally, over the years during the course of the concession agreement,
RCG completed numerous capital improvements to the facility totaling $164,050.

The initial concession agreement with RCG was for a five year term, expiring October 1, 2005.
In June 2005, the parties approved a restated concession agreement that included an option of
five (5), one-year additional terms. Before October 1st of each year, the concessionaire was
to notify the City of its intent to exercise the one-year option for the following year, in essence
providing one-year advance notice of intent to continue the agreement.

In June 2007, RCG Management forwarded a letter advising that they did not intend to exercise
the next one-year option, which meant that in the absence of a renegotiated concession
agreement, the current agreement between RCG and the City would terminate effective
October 1, 2008. Unable to renegotiate an extension, staff prepared a Request for Proposals
(RFP) to transition to a new stable operator.

Request for Proposals (RFP)

In consultation with City Council Stable Liaisons (Mayor Pro Tem Perkins and
Councilmember Humphrey), the City issued the RFP on September 26, 2008. A copy of the
RFP is included as Attachment B to this report. Because of the specialized nature of stable
operations, the City advertised the RFP on equestrian based websites and provided copies of
the RFP to RCG and to local boarders who had expressed a possible interest in submitting a
proposal. While four private parties participated in the required walk-through of the stables,
the City received one proposal by the submittal deadline. The proposal, submitted by
wife/husband combination – Erin Isom-McLewee and David McLewee, was from HGS
Management LLC.

  Page 2 of 6

  002
 Contract with HGS Management

The proposal by HGS Management specified that Ms. Isom would be on site to
oversee/manage the stables. Over the subsequent years, Mr. McLewee has handled the
business/management of the facility while Ms. Isom has focused primarily on providing
equestrian lessons and training. As reported at the award of the agreement, Ms. Isom is
knowledgeable and experienced in stable operations. She previously managed two stable
facilities in Arizona for five years from 1998 to 2003, and thereafter for the past five years, she
has managed private property known as Canyon Ranch in Rolling Hills Estates. In addition,
Ms. Isom was reported as an accomplished jumper and advanced level trainer of English riders.

In January 2014, pursuant to the concession agreement, HGS Management was provided a five
(5) year extension through February 28, 2019 for operation and management of the Stables.
Attachment C provides the staff report at the time and Attachment D provides the Stables
Concession Requirements Checklist that qualified the concessionaire for the extension. At the
time, while noting no dissatisfaction with HGS’ service but also not wanting to be committed
to an automatic second 5-year extension (to February 28, 2024), the City Council directed staff
to schedule a discussion about the future use and operations of the Stables approximately one-
to two-years before the current extension expires.

Over the subsequent years since 2014, a variety of administrative updates have been made to
the concession agreement culminating with a “revised and amendment” agreement effective
March 1, 2016 (please see: current Concession Agreement). The 2016 agreement included a
typographical error in regard to the term of the concession agreement that has since been
corrected, in a very cooperative manner with HGS Management, by the side letter listed as
Attachment E.

Since 2013, the City has received periodic complaints about the management of the Stables,
condition of stalls, and in particular, time publically available for use of the riding rings. The
issues raised have not been a violation of the Concession Agreement. Moreover, while HGS
has been responsive to them, current City officials have also been advised that the number of
complaints and issues associated with the facility are dramatically less than prior to HGS’
management. The City has not had any problems with HGS Management and continues to be
satisfied that HGS Management is in compliance with the Concession Agreement. At times,
however, their administrative response to matters (e.g., submission of budget materials and
handbook update) may be slow.

The operation of the Stables has resulted in concession fees to the City in the range of $25,000
to $35,000 in revenue compared to $18,956 during the last year of operation by RCG
Management. The revenue received by the City is equal to 5% of HGS Management’s
revenues. HGS Management has also operated the stable at close to full capacity. The only
exception was a period in 2016 when the trail operator ceased working at the facility due to
rule violations, according to HGS Management.

Since 2009 HGS Management reports improvements to, and investment in, the stables of an
average of $20,000 a year. During that time, HGS Management requested the City to contribute
toward improvements once, in 2013, for the installation of new arena lighting. The cost was
$42,124; the City contributed $17,500 from the Stable Fund.

  Page 3 of 6

  003
 Condition of Stables

The Palos Verdes Stables, located at the end of Via Opata, is situated on top of a ridge adjacent
to Valmonte Canyon to the south, west and north. Drainage and the retention of storm water
are necessary to address due to this location and the nature of the operations. As such, for
equestrian safety, protection of the environment, and slope stability, a variety of infrastructure
improvements to control runoff are necessary; areas of focus include wash-rack water, manure
containment, and slope drainage.

Structures at the Stables, with some exceptions, appear to be in generally good condition. The
City attempted to have a facility assessment completed approximately two years ago but the
effort was unsuccessful at the time due to not finding a consultant with expertise in evaluating
the capital assets of a stable facility. In the meantime, the City’s Building Inspector has visited
the property. He notes that the perimeter in/out stalls are old and in poor condition, and the
interior of some box stalls have evidence of rust. City staff also sees that the storage area for
shavings, manure and hay, and the caretaker’s residence should be improved for both aesthetics
and operations. Additionally, while HGS Management has made parking improvements for
accommodating disabled persons, other improvements are necessary.

A variety of infrastructure enhancements, including improvements to the pipe stalls, the riding
rings and lighting, have been made by the concessionaire at the facility over the past eight (8)
years; these have benefited the facility in general as well as enhanced management’s operations
and services.

The Planning Commission approved a Conditional Use Permit 96-17 on September 19, 2017
authorizing certain existing and proposed improvements at the Palos Verdes Stables.
Specifically, CUP 96-17 authorizes a new structure for hay and manure storage area. The
applicant is proposing a new approximate 1,250 sq. ft. shade structure at the northwest portion
of the property adjacent to the canyon area. The structure will consists of a 16 ft. high pre-
engineered metal building and will be used as a storage area for hay and manure. The project
is proposed to address contamination runoff into the canyon per stormwater requirements. The
project also includes authorizing existing improvements on the property such as the
Eurowalker adding and extending parking stalls and providing drainage improvements.

The City initially budgeted $35,000 in FY 2014-15 to allow for the City to construct a manure
loading platform for the storage and disposal of manure. A number of plans have been explored
and deemed infeasible. The City again budgeted $35,000 for the Manure Loading Platform in
the FY 2016-17 budget, however; the funds were not re-budgeted for FY 2017-18. With
approval to proceed and the appropriation of funds, HGS Management’s proposed capital
projects budget will provide funds to cover any overage beyond the City’s resources. Staff will
work with HGS to process the necessary permit applications. Upon development of final plans,
the City Council will be requested to reallocate the necessary funds.

For discussion, the existing agreement attributes all capital improvements such as those noted
herein are the responsibility of the concessionaire. Staff believes the stormwater requirements
extend into the City’s responsibility. HGS Management has spoken of their commitment to

  Page 4 of 6

  004
 make the comprehensive and necessary infrastructure improvements; however, progress has
been slow.

Public Status of Palos Verdes Stables

The Palos Verdes Stables is a public facility that provides for resident and non-resident
boarding of horses, equestrian training, and scheduled use of the riding rings. Instruction is
primarily focused on English style riding. HGS Management previously provided for trail
rides; trail rides are intended to begin again along with Western style instruction. A summer
camp program for children is also provided.

Current resident and non-resident use of the facility is represented in Attachment G.

DISCUSSION

The Palos Verdes Stables (Stables) requires infrastructure improvements for management and
control of storm water and protecting the surrounding slope from erosion. As noted above, a
variety of other improvements at the facility are also beneficial for the long-term viability of
stable operations. The responsibility for improvements lies within the agreement with the
concessionaire, and is anticipated to necessitate a significant investment of time and money.
The current agreement with HGS Management concludes on February 28, 2019 at which time
the City Council has the option of extending it with HGS Management for one additional 5-
year term, negotiating a revised agreement with HGS Management, issuing a new Request for
Proposals (RFP), or ceasing the use of the property as a stable. For the latter two options
identified, appropriate notice should be provided to HGS Management.

If the City were to consider repurposing the Stables property to an alternate public use, an
assessment of options would be recommended. It is recommended that the process involve a
comprehensive community engagement strategy that includes residents and property owners
in the vicinity of the Stables as well as the public at large. The assessment would be to evaluate
options for use of the property and structures as well as the improvements and demolition
needed for the change in use. A Feasibility Report would be recommended and an
environmental analysis would also likely be necessary. Closing the Stables with no alternative
uses to commence is not recommended, as the site could become an attractive nuisance and
significant maintenance responsibility for the City. At this time, funding and a funding source
has not been identified to conduct a Feasibility Study or maintain the property.

The purpose of this staff report is to have an initial, preliminary discussion of the alternatives
for moving forward. Staff requests a beginning discussion for direction on:

A) How to address the concession agreement with HGS Management (for extension,
  renegotiation or termination in February 2019), or

B) If the City should begin consideration of repurposing the property to an alternative public
  use and how to proceed.

This is intended to be the first of several discussions on this subject matter.

  Page 5 of 6

  005
 ALTERNATIVES

1. Begin discussing the options identified herein and provide direction to staff.

2. Decline to act.

NOTIFICATION

Notification of this workshop agenda topic was in the standard manner through posting of the
agenda with the staff report available on the City’s website. In addition, notice of this meeting
and a copy of the staff report was posted on the bulletin board at the Palos Verdes Stables.
HGS Management was also informed of this agenda item.

RECOMMENDATION

It is recommended that the City initiate a discussion about the use of PV Stables property, and
the extension of the concessionaire operations and management of the PV Stables, as of
February 28, 2019 when the existing agreement concludes.

Residents Protest Plans for Palos
Verdes Estates Stable
Recreation: Proposals to privatize city-owned
horse facility angers those fearing loss of public
uses.
April 28, 2000|JESSICA GARRISON | SPECIAL TO THE TIMES

A hoof-stamping, tail-swishing fight is brewing in Palos Verdes Estates over who will
take the reins of the beloved city-owned horse stables.

Since 1926, the city has run a 60-stall facility, tucked into a canyon on the eastern edge
of town. There beneath shade trees, the jodphur-wearing, horse-owning crowd has
mixed with weekend riders who rent the few public horses for trail jaunts or lessons.
Parents can even send children afflicted with horse fever to a city-run riding school in
the summer.

Stables are scattered throughout the horsy country of the Palos Verdes Peninsula and
throughout Los Angeles County, but most are reserved for people with the money and
commitment to own horses.

Now, some Palos Verdes Estates residents fear that their stables soon may be saddled
with a similar privatized fate. They are protesting proposed changes they say could limit
the public nature of the place.

Last month, a group of horse owners, complaining about crowding and poor
maintenance, asked the City Council to turn management of the stables over to them.

The group, which is led by a local landscape businessman, promised to improve the
facility by spending $100,000 in private funds to add a third practice ring, do
landscaping work and even install a little coffee stand so parents could watch their
children ride in style.

But they also talked about eliminating the daily rental rides and the city-run summer
camp that serves about 200 youngsters.

The council this week heard public debate about that proposal and several other
competing ideas for the stables. A decision is expected as early as next month.

  Page 1 of 3

  007
 Many boarders say that turning the stables over to a private group is the perfect solution
for upkeep and finances.

Though its stalls are occupied and have a waiting list for boarders, the riding center in
recent years has made an annual profit of about $24,000--not enough to pay for long-
term upkeep.

"We need a place to go in Palos Verdes to enjoy our expensive hobby," resident Michelle
Bryan told council members Tuesday night. Bryan said she has moved her horse out of
town because he was receiving substandard care.

But opponents of private management have stampeded City Council meetings and
corralled neighbors to sign petitions.

"Many of our children and grandchildren cannot afford to buy homes in PVE. They also
cannot afford to own their own horses, but they return to the stable and bring their own
children to benefit from the activities they once enjoyed," said resident Scottie Wuerker.
"I want to make sure my grandchildren can still ride there, and once they've handed this
over to a profit-making corporation, the city is not going to have control."

Palos Verdes Estates Mayor Chad Turner called the situation "a migraine headache."

While there are six proposals, most observers agree that two of them are the most likely
choices. One calls for the city to keep control of the property, but change the operation
somewhat to make it more profitable. The other would keep public ownership but bring
in a private operator, headed by landscaper Bob Gaudenti's company GS Brothers Inc.

Gaudenti originally proposed ending the summer camp and trail rides and cutting
lesson hours from 90 a week to 30. But heeding protesters' concerns, some City Council
members said they would require any plan retain those services.

Gaudenti said opponents' suggestion that he wants to manage the stables to turn a profit
is "laughable."

"This is our hobby, not our business," Gaudenti said. "We just want to clean the place
up, make improvements. Right now, boarders are treated like second-class citizens."

But some residents say they just don't believe things will stay the same under different
management.

"My concern is that it isn't going to be nearly as accessible as it has been in the past,"
said John Howe, who started coming to the stable this year with his 8-year-old daughter
Morgan.

Now, father and daughter each week scramble up on the city's lesson horses to trot and
canter. "I know verbal promises have been made, but once such a facility comes under

  Page 2 of 3

  008
 the control of a private corporation, the reality is that they will be in a position to dictate
and control how it is operated," Howe said.

Like many boarders, John Ollen, who has kept his horses at the stable for the past 20
years, said he doesn't care who runs the stable, as long as children whose families don't
have horses can learn to ride there.

"The stables are a place of refuge," he told council members. "They bring back a quieter,
more genteel time, and they represent something that is vanishing very quickly in our
society."

With 72 stalls, 1 is empty and 27 are occupied by residents. Forty-four are occupied by non-residents. One of
the trainers has 8 horses in the lesson program that are available to residents and non-residents if they have no
horse.

The intermediate lesson program provides an average of 682 lessons a month of which 231 are lessons to
residents and 451 to non-residents. These are not unique clients in that many of them have 3 lessons a week
while some have 1 lesson per week.

The three trainers involved in the beginning lesson program average 210 lessons a month of which 62 are
resident lessons and 148 are non-resident lessons. These are not unique clients as many of them ride twice a
week.

One trainer specifically trains in dressage and gives 62 lessons a month, of which all are residents.

The stables has one trainer that only focuses on boarders that have a horse and board at Palos Verdes Stables.
Lessons are provided to 25 boarders who take 3 lessons a week which is 325 lessons a month. 163 lessons are
given to residents and 162 are non resident lessons.

The 2017 summer camp had 106 participants this year. Sixty-five were residents although many attended more
than once, and 41 were non-residents.

There are 7 boarders that don’t take any type of lessons.
